sources.title: Henry J. Heinz (Q982831), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-06): label 'Henry J. Heinz', description 'American businessman (1844-1919)', Korean label 헨리 J. 하인즈, born 11 October 1844, died 14 May 1919, citizenship United States. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Senator John Heinz History Center, collection page 'H.J. Heinz Company' (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: company founded in 1869 by Henry John Heinz as a horseradish producer in Sharpsburg; the first business failed after the Panic of 1873 and he re-established it in 1876 with help from his brother John and cousin Frederick; tomato ketchup followed in 1876; he took control in 1888 and the H.J. Heinz Company name began; factories and branches in the 1890s and by 1905 incorporation and factories in England and Spain; he lobbied in favour of the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 and pioneered efforts to maintain cleanliness and quality; he took a notably progressive attitude to employees; at his death in 1919 the company had 6,500 employees and 25 branch factories. Institutional collection description, favourable in tone.

Robert C. Alberts, 'The Good Provider: H. J. Heinz and His 57 Varieties', American Heritage 23(2), February 1972 (magazine excerpt from Alberts's biography, read in full; quotes his private diary). Clear glass horseradish bottles against adulterated rivals; the 1875 over-extension and bankruptcy (assets $110,000, liabilities $170,000) and the 1876 restart as F. & J. Heinz; seed-and-buy contracts with pickle growers (1880); the 1886 call on Fortnum & Mason with no introduction; the factory with its employee facilities and open plant tours; the '57 Varieties' slogan (1896, by this account) and the 1893 Chicago fair stunt; support for the 1906 food laws; the company's size at his death. Admiring biographer who also records the paternalism-and-no-union aim and that 57 was a sales slogan; largely a self-diary-derived narrative.

Brian Butko, 'Heinz: Much More than 57 Varieties', Senator John Heinz History Center blog, 12 May 2015 (read in full). COUNTER-VOICE: says Heinz was scorned in the 1870s for poor business decisions, that his business was short of capital and collapsed and that he was arrested on creditors' fraud charges, then rebuilt on the family's moral lessons; describes the plant's restaurant, dressing rooms, hospital, gymnasium, rooftop garden, classes and work-time carriage rides; dates the 57 Varieties phrase to 1892 (Alberts says 1896, so the slogan date is not used). Institutional author, local museum.

The Henry Ford, curated set 'Henry J. Heinz: His Recipe for Success' (read in full). 'Strictly Pure' label of 1872 and clear glass against rivals' coloured containers; recipe notebook and tasting rooms for consistency; partnering with growers and building branch factories near farms; the Pittsburgh plant deemed a model factory with awards for 'industrial betterment'; says he became an advocate for the Pure Food and Drug Act. Museum set text, celebratory; mostly object captions.

Pittsburgh Quarterly, 'Make No Little Plans' (article on Pittsburgh at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition; only the Heinz passage was read, quoting a History Center curator). Heinz's exhibit stood on the second floor of the Agriculture Building, so he hired boys to hand out tags offering a 'novel watch charm' to anyone who came to the booth; crowds came in droves, the other food exhibitors gave him a silver loving cup, and the pickle charm became the pickle pin. Regional magazine; one passage only.

Elizabeth Lewis Otey, 'Employers' Welfare Work', Bulletin of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics No. 123, 1913 (US government report, FRASER digital copy; the H. J. Heinz Co. section on pp. 33-34 and the introduction read). INDEPENDENT AND CRITICAL-CONTEXT SOURCE: describes the Heinz welfare work (clean uniforms, manicurist, dining room with coffee at 1 cent, free woman physician, lockers, picnic, roof garden, natatorium, classes, a premium for good work, a sick-benefit association) but explains much of it as a necessity of handling food, and its introduction records labour circles' complaint that welfare work is tinctured with paternalism and dependence on the employer's goodwill.

Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery, object record NPG.93.388.14, 'Henry John Heinz' by Pach Brothers Studio, c. 1914, gelatin silver print (read via the Smithsonian Open Access API). Portrait source record for the image used; rights field 'CC0'.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_heinz_alberts, src_heinz_henryford, src_heinz_hhcblog | 1860s-1890s | biographer excerpt, museum set, museum blog] He packed horseradish in clear glass against rivals' coloured bottles and adulterated roots, built a line of prepared condiments for households, sold his first goods to a London fine-food house in 1886 and later opened branches abroad, and built the exhibit and plant tours that made the brand known. The sources agree on the pattern of finding a gap in how processed food was sold, but all are celebratory or from one narrative lineage, with no sceptical economic study read. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.55 to 68 / 0.50 because the institutional texts repeat the biographer's framing and no independent economic assessment was read.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_heinz_pq, src_heinz_alberts | 1876, 1893 | regional magazine passage, biographer excerpt] After the 1875 bankruptcy he restarted as manager of his brother's and cousin's firm on borrowed capital and, by his own diary, bought a cheap horse to get through a pinch; at the 1893 Chicago fair, with his exhibit stranded on an upstairs gallery, he handed out tags promising a free charm so that crowds climbed to his booth. The fair episode is told consistently by two sources but is one incident, and the restart is mostly his own diary via the biographer. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.55 to 66 / 0.50 because the fair stunt is a single incident retold by several sources, not independent instances.

persistence.rationale: [src_heinz_alberts, src_heinz_hhc, src_heinz_hhcblog | 1875-1888 | biographer excerpt, two History Center texts] The first firm failed in 1875 (Alberts: assets $110,000, liabilities $170,000; the History Center says it failed after the Panic of 1873 and that he was arrested on creditors' fraud charges), yet he was manager of the new F. & J. Heinz in 1876 and bought control of the business in 1888. The restart is documented by independent institutional and biographical sources; the claim that he later repaid creditors out of his salary rests on his diary through Alberts only and is not relied on, and the fraud arrest shows the episode was contested. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): persistence lowered from 70 / 0.6 to 66 / 0.54 because the failure-and-restart account is one biographer plus an institutional blog, and the diary is self-report.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_heinz_alberts, src_heinz_henryford | 1880-1919 | biographer excerpt, museum set] He contracted growers to take his cucumber seed and sell him the harvest (1880), built branch factories and receiving stations near the farms, and by 1919 the company owned a seed farm, can and bottle plants and its own rail cars. The sources describe a deliberate supply-chain plan, but both are favourable and the scale figures come from the same narrative.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_heinz_henryford, src_heinz_alberts, src_heinz_bls1913 | 1872-1913 | museum set, biographer excerpt, government report] A recipe notebook and tasting rooms to keep the flavour consistent, a steel tape measure and diary kept on every trip, a fireproof, electrically lit stable and a plant where sanitation (clean uniforms, manicures for women handling food, supplied soap and towels) was systematic. The government report ties the sanitation to the needs of food handling, so the detail work is documented as practice but its personal intensity is only moderately evidenced.

social_assertiveness.rationale: [src_heinz_alberts | 1886 | biographer excerpt from his diary] On his first trip to London he walked into Fortnum & Mason with no letter of introduction, asked for the head of grocery purchasing and opened his sample bag; the buyer took all seven lines. One diary-based anecdote told by an admiring biographer. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.45 to 60 / 0.40 because the row rests on a single anecdote from his own diary retold by one admiring source.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_heinz_alberts, src_heinz_hhcblog | 1875 | biographer excerpt, museum blog] In 1875 he and Noble committed to pickle the crop of some 600 acres of cucumbers on credit while already overextended; Alberts says he mortgaged his house and his father's brick kiln and the firm failed, and the History Center says he was scorned for poor business decisions and arrested on creditors' fraud charges. The over-commitment is documented by two sources and the later growth shows the same appetite for large commitments, so the impact is dual-edged.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_heinz_alberts, src_heinz_bls1913, src_heinz_hhc | 1890s-1913 | biographer excerpt, government report, museum text] He funded employee facilities, free medical care, classes and open plant tours and backed the 1906 food law; but the government report explains the welfare work largely as a necessity of handling food and records labour circles' paternalism objection, and Alberts reports he hoped the facilities would stop his workers striking. A real concern for conditions and public confidence is documented, but the motive is mixed, hence a modest score, low confidence and dual-edged impact.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead-robust) (lead) / CONFIRMED BUT LEAD REPLACED. The lead's Bain 1917 photograph (LoC) could not be verified at the holder (loc.gov bot-walled) and its Commons file is a head-and-shoulders crop from a six-man group photograph (ggbain.25508) that still shows neighbours' sleeves and a standing man's jacket, with only a generic PD-US tag; the Columbus Metropolitan Library 1913 slide was checked on Commons only. I therefore used a better route: the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery's studio portrait by Pach Brothers Studio (c. 1914, NPG.93.388.14), whose holder record (Smithsonian Open Access API) states 'Restrictions & Rights: CC0' and names the sitter; Commons agrees (CC0 template, source the NPG). HOLDER RECORD CHECKED: edanmdm:npg_NPG.93.388.14, CC0, image 3101x4000, no contradiction. INSCRIPTION CHECK: I looked at the downscaled image; it is a clean three-quarter-length studio portrait of an elderly man with white hair and moustache, with no caption, signature, label or lettering, so identity rests on the museum's record (sitter named in the record) and matches the 1917 Bain crop and the 1913 slide in appearance; no contradiction. KIND: likeness (a studio sitting). Downscaled 3101x4000 to 930x1200 (no upscaling, no crop; the sheet edge is visible) and saved as public/portraits/henry-john-heinz-pach-brothers-1914.jpg. No private-life, health or motive inference beyond what the sources state about his business conduct. HISTORICAL ATTRIBUTION (lead screen: attributable): CONFIRMED (attribution_confirmed true); documented in a diary-based biography excerpt, institutional records and a government report. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Senator John Heinz History Center collection page 'H.J. Heinz Company' (https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/research/collection-highlights/h-j-heinz-company/). READ (6 substantive sources plus Wikidata and the NPG record): (1) the History Center collection page; (2) Alberts, American Heritage 1972 (read in full); (3) History Center blog by Butko; (4) The Henry Ford curated set; (5) Pittsburgh Quarterly (the Heinz passage only); (6) US Bureau of Labor Statistics Bulletin 123 (1913), the Heinz section and introduction. PERSPECTIVES: a diary-based biographer, two museums (History Center, Henry Ford), a regional magazine citing a curator, and an independent 1913 government labour-statistics report. COUNTER-VOICES AND LIMITS: the History Center blog says he was scorned for poor business decisions and arrested on creditors' fraud charges after the first collapse, the BLS report attributes much of the welfare work to the needs of food handling and records labour's paternalism objection, and Alberts himself says the facilities aimed to prevent strikes and that there was no union for 45 years. DATE CONFLICTS: the 57 Varieties slogan is dated 1896 (Alberts) and 1892 (History Center blog), so no slogan date is stated in the cards; the cause of the first failure differs (Panic of 1873 or 1875 credit crisis). NOT OPENED: Skrabec's 2009 biography, Alberts's full 1973 book, a Pure Food Act scholarly history naming Heinz (so the political side is not scored), Britannica (bot-walled), the Encyclopedia.com Gale entry (read but not used: its story of a horseradish price collapse contradicts the better sources). EXCLUSIONS: politics and lobbying as activism, religion, family, his health and death, his mansion and museum, and the factory-tour and welfare claims of 'first' wording except where a source states it. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): rows reviewed: opportunity_sensing (72/0.55 lowered to 68/0.50: institutional texts repeat the biographer's framing), resourcefulness (70/0.55 lowered to 66/0.50: the 1893 stunt is one incident retold several times), social_assertiveness (64/0.45 lowered to 60/0.40: single diary anecdote via one admiring source), persistence (70/0.6 kept: the failure and restart are documented by independent institutional and biographical sources). MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT SELF-GATE: first-pass PASS on primary, top omission, identity, significance-over-novelty and side-project; nothing corrected. Card 1 states the founding and growth of the Heinz company and its branded marketing, card 2 the pure-product and food-law stance, card 3 the model factory.
